title: How Mirrors Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and physics of mirrors. They cover early polished obsidian mirrors in Anatolia around 6000 BC, metal mirrors of silver, bronze and copper, and the later glass mirror with silvering invented by Justus von Liebig in 1835. They discuss mirrors' influence on self-portraits and linear perspective (Brunelleschi), reflecting telescopes, and the Archimedes death ray legend (MythBusters). The physics segment covers the law of reflection, specular versus diffuse reflection, virtual images, the Venus effect, and why mirrors seem to reverse left and right. They then discuss concave and convex mirrors, the nonreversing mirror, two-way mirrors, horror and movie mirror tropes, mirror superstitions and mourning customs, and Chinese mirror-kingdom folklore. The episode closes with a listener mail about a New York City Walk to Beat Lung Cancer.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about childhood mirror habits and body image, then introduce the topic of mirrors.

segments.title: History of mirrors
segments.summary: Early mirrors were polished obsidian from Anatolia around 6000 BC, later made of heavy polished metal that limited size and was costly. Glass mirrors improved with Venetian techniques, and Liebig's silvering process in 1835 produced the modern mirror. Venetian mirror-making was a closely guarded secret.

segments.title: Mirrors, art and science
segments.summary: Good mirrors arrived alongside linear perspective in art, which Brunelleschi is credited with, and made self-portraits possible. Mirrors were also used in reflecting telescopes, and the hosts discuss the Archimedes death ray legend and MythBusters' test.

segments.title: Law of reflection and the Venus effect
segments.summary: Chuck explains the law of reflection, angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, and why sunsets glare. Josh explains specular versus diffuse reflection and virtual images. They discuss the Venus effect in paintings and the apparent left-right reversal, which is really front-back reversal.

segments.title: Curved, nonreversing and two-way mirrors
segments.summary: Convex mirrors widen the field of view on car mirrors. Concave mirrors project real images used in holograms and lighting the Olympic torch. Nonreversing mirrors are two perpendicular mirrors, and John Derby held a patent for one. Two-way mirrors reflect partly and transmit partly depending on lighting.

segments.title: Mirrors in movies, folklore and customs
segments.summary: Movie mirror and two-way mirror tropes are discussed, along with Poltergeist's mirror scene. Superstitions include Bloody Mary, breaking mirrors and seven years of bad luck, and vampires. Jewish mourning custom of covering mirrors during shiva is mentioned, along with New Year's Eve and Chinese mirror-kingdom folklore.

segments.title: Listener mail: Walk to Beat Lung Cancer
segments.summary: A listener promotes the New York City Walk to Beat Lung Cancer in Battery Park in October 2010 and argues lung cancer funding is stigmatized.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode with a pitch to send organization mail and a sponsor read.
